title: The Presocratics
note: The first Greek philosophers sought the arche, the basic source or principle of all things, and explained nature by reasons rather than myth. Monists named one stuff (water, the boundless, air); pluralists named several. Heraclitus stressed constant change; Parmenides argued that real being cannot change at all.

read.title: From myth to reason
text: In the sixth century BCE, thinkers in the Greek city of Miletus asked a new kind of question: what is everything made of, and why does it change? Thales answered water. Anaximander proposed an unlimited stuff, the apeiron, from which hot and cold and the other opposites separate. Anaximenes chose air, which becomes fire when thinned and stone when packed tight. Their answers were wrong, but their method was new. They gave natural causes that could be argued about, not stories about gods.

Two later thinkers sharpened the debate. Heraclitus taught that everything flows, like a river whose water is always new, yet the change follows a rational pattern he called the logos. Parmenides argued the opposite. Whatever truly is cannot come from nothing or pass into nothing, so real being is one and unchanging, and the senses that report change deceive us. His student Zeno built paradoxes to show how strange motion becomes when examined closely.

Later pluralists tried to save both sides. Empedocles kept unchanging elements but let Love and Strife rearrange them. The atomists said changeless atoms move through empty space, and their shifting arrangements produce the changing world we see.
